guide.title: Chapter 3 — Public Fire Protection
guide.course: Introduction to Fire Protection and Emergency Services
guide.overview: This chapter traces how organized fire protection grew from bucket brigades and Roman slave patrols into today's all-hazards emergency services agency. It covers the equipment and gear that made modern firefighting possible, the history of wildland fire policy in America, the disasters that shaped building codes and standards, and the statistics that define the U.S. fire problem. It closes with the modern purpose of the fire service: managing community risk through prevention, education, planning, and response.
big_picture: Most fire-service reforms came after a disaster: Rome's Vigiles, London's building codes, standardized hose threads after Baltimore, and national suppression policy after the Big Blowup.
Firefighting in America moved from bucket brigades to insurance brigades, to volunteer companies, to paid departments, driven largely by the steam engine and by rowdy competition among volunteers.
Wildland fire policy swung from 'put every fire out by 10 a.m.' to managing fire as a natural process, because fuel buildup makes future fires worse.
The U.S. has one of the highest fire death rates per capita in the industrialized world, and most civilian fire deaths happen at home.
The main purpose of today's fire service is managing community risk, not just putting out fires. Prevention, education, and planning matter as much as response.

sections.heading: Fire and Humanity
sections.simplified:
Humans are the only creatures that learned to start and use fire, likely somewhere between 200,000 and 400,000 years ago. Controlling fire changed everything. It let people live in colder places, cook and store food, make tools and pottery, and eventually settle down instead of wandering for food.

Fire also powered the Industrial Revolution in the 1700s, because steam power comes from heat. Fire has always been a weapon of war too, from burning enemy crops in ancient times to the British burning Washington, D.C. in 1814. The chapter's warning: problems start when people get too comfortable with fire and stop respecting it, and that danger grew as people moved into crowded cities.
key_points: Humans are the only species that learned to start and use fire.
Evidence suggests people began using fire 200,000–400,000 years ago.
Controlled fire let people live in colder areas, store food, and form permanent settlements.
The Industrial Revolution (18th century) began with steam power generated by controlled fire.
Fire has long been used as a weapon: the British burned Washington, D.C. in 1814 during the War of 1812.
As people became city dwellers, fire became more destructive, and the fire service evolved to deal with it.
remember: People learned to use fire roughly 200,000–400,000 years ago.
Problems arise when people become too comfortable with fire and lose respect for it.

sections.heading: Early Firefighting: Rome to the American Colonies
sections.simplified:
The first organized firefighting force was in ancient Rome. It was called the Familia Publica and was made up of slaves, who were slow to respond. After several disastrous fires, Emperor Augustus created the Corps of Vigiles: 7,000 men in battalions of 1,000, publicly funded, who patrolled the streets, fought fires with buckets and axes, and warned citizens to be careful. People who carelessly started fires could be physically punished.

In America, Jamestown was nearly wiped out by fire in 1608, just a year after it was founded, because homes were built of flammable materials and packed close together. Early colonists fought fire with bucket brigades and by pulling buildings down to make firebreaks. Peter Stuyvesant of New Amsterdam (later New York) wrote a building code banning wood or plaster chimneys, appointed fire wardens, and set up the 'rattle watch' to patrol at night.

After the Great Fire of London in 1666, fire insurance companies started their own fire brigades, but they only protected buildings they insured. Boston created America's first publicly funded, paid fire department in 1679, and Benjamin Franklin organized the Union Volunteer Fire Company in Philadelphia in 1736, the model for today's volunteer companies.
key_points: Rome's Familia Publica (slaves with primitive pumps) was the first recognized firefighting force.
Emperor Augustus formed the Corps of Vigiles: 7,000 men, 1,000 per battalion, publicly funded, freedom after six years of service.
Jamestown (founded 1607) nearly failed after a conflagration in 1608: combustible materials plus closely spaced buildings.
Colonial fire protection: firebreaks made by pulling down structures, and bucket brigades.
1647: Peter Stuyvesant banned wood or plaster chimneys, appointed four fire wardens, and created the rattle watch; towns imposed a 9:00 p.m.–4:30 a.m. fire curfew.
Great Fire of London (1666) burned for five days, destroyed about two-thirds of the city, and led to building codes and fire insurance companies.
Insurance-company brigades only fought fires at the properties they insured.
Early water mains were hollowed-out logs; firefighters pulled a wooden plug to reach the water.
remember: 1679 — Boston: first publicly funded, paid fire department in America.
1736 — Ben Franklin: Union Volunteer Fire Company in Philadelphia.
Corps of Vigiles — formed by Augustus; 7,000 men in battalions of 1,000.
London 1666 reforms: wider streets, green spaces, building setbacks, noncombustible materials.

sections.heading: Volunteers, Paid Departments, and the Modern Fire Service
sections.simplified:
After the Revolutionary War, volunteer fire companies spread across the country. Membership was a point of pride, and famous Americans like George Washington, John Hancock, Alexander Hamilton, Samuel Adams, and Paul Revere served. The companies were fiercely competitive. Crews literally fist-fought over who got 'first water' on a fire. That rowdiness pushed cities toward paid departments, and in 1853 Cincinnati became the first city with a fully paid fire department.

Today's fire department is proactive rather than waiting for alarms. It provides fire prevention, public education, suppression, medical aid, rescue, and hazardous materials response. Medical calls can be 70 percent of a department's incidents. Tradition is strong, with red engines and working your way up from the bottom, but the chapter argues the service must also adapt.

Stations changed as paid firefighters lived there around the clock, adding sleeping quarters and the sliding pole. Protective gear evolved from street clothes to uniforms, the long-tailed helmet, insulated turnout gear, and finally the self-contained breathing apparatus, or SCBA, invented around 1945.
key_points: Volunteer companies spread after the Revolutionary War and were intensely competitive over 'first water.'
1853: Cincinnati became the first city with a fully paid fire department.
Modern services: prevention, public education, suppression, medical aid, rescue, and hazardous materials.
Some departments report medical aid is 70% of their incident volume.
Fire stations added sleeping quarters and sliding poles (wood, then brass) once paid firefighters were on duty 24 hours.
Helmet design: short front brim, long back brim to keep embers and water off the neck; ribs added for rigidity.
Breathing protection went from wet rags or beards, to canister gas masks, to modern SCBA around 1945.
remember: 1853 — Cincinnati: first fully paid fire department.
SCBA (self-contained breathing apparatus) was invented around 1945 and made interior attack possible.
Gas masks filtered smoke particles but did not protect against toxic gases or low oxygen.

sections.heading: History of Wildland Fire in America
sections.simplified:
Native tribes used fire on purpose: to herd buffalo, renew vegetation, and clear the forest floor. Those burns left forests with bigger trees, less undergrowth, and richer soil. Settlement changed that. Logging and land clearing altered rivers and forests, and the transcontinental railroad, finished in 1869, left piles of dried logging slash along the tracks while spark-throwing wood-fired trains crossed the country.

The deadliest wildland fire in U.S. history was at Peshtigo, Wisconsin, in 1871, killing more than 1,500 people. Two fires shaped national policy. The Big Blowup of 1910 burned over 3 million acres in two days in Idaho and Montana, and led to the Weeks Act of 1911 and a policy of suppressing every fire by 10 a.m. the next day. Later, national parks adopted a let-burn policy for lightning fires. The 1988 Yellowstone fires, managed under that policy, burned far more than expected and cost 112 million dollars, yet the park has since thrived.

Today the debate is about fuel reduction. Federal agencies 'manage' fires on their land by weighing cost, safety, and resource values, which can confuse local firefighters used to putting out every fire. Lightning starts the largest fires, but humans cause up to 90 percent of wildland fires.
key_points: Native Americans burned land to herd buffalo, renew vegetation, and reduce undergrowth.
Burning reduced fuel loading, returned nutrients to the soil, and favored large trees.
The transcontinental railroad (1869) created fire hazards: logging slash along tracks and sparks from wood-fired boilers.
Peshtigo, Wisconsin (1871): deadliest U.S. wildland fire, over 1,500 killed, 2,400 square miles burned.
Big Blowup (1910): over 3 million acres in two days, at least 85 killed, smoke reached Boston.
Weeks Act (1911) funded Forest Service cooperation with states; policy was to suppress every fire by 10 a.m. the next day.
Yellowstone (1988): 13 fires, about 800,000 acres in the park, 112 million dollars to suppress, managed under let-burn.
Motorized equipment such as chainsaws and bulldozers is not allowed on congressionally designated wilderness land.
remember: Peshtigo, 1871 — greatest loss-of-life wildland fire in U.S. history (1,500+ deaths).
The Big Blowup (1910) and Yellowstone (1988) are the two fires that most changed national wildland policy.
The '10 a.m. policy': every fire out by 10 a.m. the next day.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Firefighting Equipment
sections.simplified:
Equipment evolved because growing cities needed better ways to get water onto fires. The first known fire pump, the siphona, was invented in the third century BC. It used two pistons and an air chamber to push out a steady stream, and the same idea later powered hand pumpers into the twentieth century.

Hand pumpers were worked by crews on long handles called brakes, pumping 60 to 170 strokes a minute. Adding hose to the nozzle, called the gooseneck, let crews attack from different angles and gave birth to the interior attack. Hose went from sewn leather, to riveted leather, to linen, rubber-lined cotton, and today's synthetics.

The steamer was the next big leap. It needed only three people, pumped as long as it had coal, and was pulled by horses. Because cities no longer needed big volunteer crews, the steamer helped end volunteer departments in large cities. Ladder companies formed as buildings got taller, the aerial ladder appeared by 1870, chemical wagons used soda and acid to make pressure, and finally the internal combustion engine took over. Today the same motor drives both the truck and the pump.
key_points: Siphona: first known fire pump, third century BC; two cylinders with pistons plus an air chamber for a steady stream.
Fire hooks pulled burning thatch off roofs and pulled down houses for firebreaks.
Hand pumper handles (brakes) were up to 15 feet long; crews pumped 60–170 strokes per minute.
Adding hose to the gooseneck gave birth to the interior attack.
A suction hose permanently attached to the pumper was called a squirrel tail.
Steamers needed only a three-person crew and helped end volunteer departments in big cities.
Ladder companies handled forcible entry, rescue, and ventilation; aerial ladders appeared by 1870.
Chemical wagons mixed soda-water and acid to create carbon dioxide pressure, fast to deploy but risky if a hose kinked.
remember: Siphona — first known fire pump (third century BC); its principle was used in hand pumpers.
Order of apparatus: hand pumper → steamer → chemical wagon → internal combustion engine.
Pike pole pulls down ceilings; pike axe is used for forcible entry.

sections.heading: Fire Service Symbols
sections.simplified:
Several symbols represent the fire service: red engines, the fire axe, Smokey Bear, and Sparky the Fire Dog. The Maltese cross is the best known. It dates to the Crusades, when Saracens threw glass bombs of naphtha at Christian knights and then set them on fire. Many died coming to their comrades' aid, and the survivors were awarded a special cross for their bravery. Many of these knights belonged to the Knights of St. John, based on the island of Malta, which gave the cross its name. It stands for protection and a willingness to lay down one's life for others.

Dalmatians became fire service mascots when horses entered firehouses. They ran alongside horse-drawn rigs and kept the horses calm.
key_points: Common fire service symbols: red engines, the fire axe, Smokey Bear, Sparky the Fire Dog.
The Maltese cross is a symbol of protection and a badge of honor.
It comes from the Knights of St. John, headquartered on Malta, honored for bravery against naphtha attacks.
Dalmatians guarded horse-drawn vehicles and kept the horses calm.
remember: Maltese cross — origin in the Crusades; Knights of St. John on Malta; symbolizes protection and self-sacrifice.
Dalmatians kept firehouse horses calm.

sections.heading: Major Fire Losses
sections.simplified:
Large fires have repeatedly devastated American cities. The Great Chicago Fire of October 8 to 10, 1871, destroyed over three square miles, left 100,000 people homeless, and killed about 300. Fires like it led President Calvin Coolidge to proclaim the first National Fire Prevention Week in October 1925, which still happens every October.

In Baltimore in 1904, crews from other cities arrived to help but their hose threads didn't fit Baltimore's hydrants, which eventually led to standardized hose threads. Across these conflagrations the common causes were combustible construction, narrow streets, and weak building codes, especially unprotected vertical shafts.

Losses are more than buildings: families lose irreplaceable belongings, and burned businesses often never reopen, costing jobs and taxes. Arson and terrorism also cause huge losses; on September 11, 2001, more than 3,000 people died, including 343 firefighters.

Wildland losses keep rising as more homes are built in the wildland-urban interface. All ten of the costliest U.S. wildland fires happened in California, driven partly by hot, dry Santa Ana winds. The 2018 Camp Fire killed 85 people and destroyed the town of Paradise. Climate change is expected to bring more floods, heat illness, disease, drought, and severe storms, all increasing the demand on responders.
key_points: Great Chicago Fire (Oct 8–10, 1871): 3⅓ square miles destroyed, 100,000 homeless, about 300 killed.
First National Fire Prevention Week: October 4–10, 1925, proclaimed by President Coolidge.
Baltimore (Feb 7, 1904): mismatched hose threads led to standardized hose threads.
Common denominators of conflagrations: combustible construction, narrow streets, ineffective building codes.
September 11, 2001: over 3,000 killed, including 343 firefighters.
Homes lost to wildland fire rose from about 250 a year to 2,700 a year since the 1960s.
Of 17 million homes built 1990–2008, 10 million were in the wildland-urban interface.
Santa Ana winds form when high pressure over the Great Basin meets low pressure off Southern California.
2007 was the most active wildland fire year since 1960: about 9.87 million acres burned.
Aviation caused 50% of wildland firefighter deaths in 2000–2010; burn-overs caused 20%.

Chicago 1871 → first Fire Prevention Week (1925, Coolidge).

sections.heading: The U.S. Fire Problem by the Numbers
sections.simplified:
Every year the National Fire Protection Association, or NFPA, uses data from the National Fire Incident Reporting System, or NFIRS, to describe the national fire problem. The U.S. has one of the highest fire death rates per capita in the industrialized world, 13.1 per million people.

About 4,000 people die in fires each year and 22,000 are injured. About 100 firefighters die in the line of duty each year. There are about 1.9 million reported fires a year, causing more than 10 billion dollars in direct property loss. Most civilian fire deaths, 82 percent, happen at home.

Know the leading causes. Cooking is the leading cause of home fires and injuries. Careless smoking is the leading cause of fire deaths. Heating equipment is second for both home fires and deaths. In commercial properties, arson leads in deaths, injuries, and dollar loss. Seniors face more than double the average risk of dying in a fire, and young children nearly double. Smoke alarms and residential sprinklers make a large difference: sprinklers cut the home fire death rate by 74 percent.
key_points: NFPA compiles data from NFIRS each year.
U.S. fire death rate: 13.1 per million, among the highest in the industrialized world.
About 4,000 civilian deaths and 22,000 injuries per year.
About 100 firefighters killed and 87,000 injured per year.
Fire is the third-leading cause of accidental death in the home.
The South and poverty-stricken areas have the highest fire and death rates.
Men are killed or injured in fires twice as often as women.
About 90% of homes have a smoke alarm, yet 60% of residential fire deaths happen in homes without one.
The fire service responds to a fire every 17 seconds; a fire death occurs every 147 minutes.
remember: Cooking = leading cause of home fires and injuries.
Careless smoking = leading cause of fire deaths.
Heating equipment = second leading cause of home fires and home fire deaths.
Arson = leading cause of deaths, injuries, and dollar loss in commercial properties.

sections.heading: Purpose and Scope of Fire Agencies
sections.simplified:
The main purpose of the fire service is to manage community risk. Since risk can never be eliminated, the goal is acceptable risk: a level where the chance of harm is small enough, or the benefit big enough, that people are willing to accept it. A community shows how seriously it takes fire risk through the resources it gives its fire department.

Modern departments cover far more than fires: emergency medical services, emergency management for disasters, rescue teams, and hazardous materials. Response alone can't prevent incidents, so departments also do public education, prevention, and code enforcement. Because they spend public money, they have to manage resources carefully and stay safe to keep injury costs down.

Fire departments manage risk in three categories: community risk, organizational risk, and operational risk during emergencies. Their responsibilities now include fire prevention inspections, smoke detector programs, public education on local hazards, hazardous materials permits and inventories, and arson investigation and cost recovery alongside law enforcement.
key_points: Main purpose of the fire service: manage community risk.
Acceptable risk: probability so small, consequences so slight, or benefits so great that people accept the risk.
A community expresses its perceived fire risk through the resources it commits to its fire department.
Three risk categories: community risk, organizational risk, operational risk.
Fire prevention bureaus review building designs, water flow requirements, and inspect occupied buildings.
Smoke detectors are cheap and have a huge life-safety impact; West Virginia's 2008 death rate (23.7 per million) was about twice the national rate.
Arson investigation and cost recovery require close work with law enforcement and prosecutors.
remember: The main purpose of the fire service is to manage community risk.
Three risk categories: community, organizational, operational.
Acceptable risk — not zero risk — is the goal.

sections.heading: Fire Defense Planning and Risk Management
sections.simplified:
Fire defense planning aims to deliver effective fire protection at the least cost. It follows a cycle: set goals, set measurable objectives, study statistics to see where you stand, set policies and procedures, provide people and equipment, get funding, then evaluate results and start again. Policies are general guidelines; procedures are specific instructions for recurring tasks.

Personnel are the biggest cost, often up to 90 percent of a career department's budget. Two NFPA standards address staffing: NFPA 1710 for career departments and NFPA 1720 for volunteer departments. Some ideas, like inspecting every home, aren't acceptable because of the Fourth Amendment and cost.

Risk is judged by two factors: how likely something is, and how bad the outcome would be. The situations to watch most closely are high in both. Risk management uses three kinds of control measures: administrative, like procedures and training; engineering, like equipment design; and personal protection, like protective gear. NFPA 1500 requires a written risk management plan with four parts. Community risk reduction has four steps: preparation, mitigation, response, and recovery.
key_points: Planning cycle: goals → objectives → statistics → policies → personnel → procedures → facilities → funding → evaluation.
Objectives must be clearly stated and measurable.
Personnel can be up to 90% of a career department's budget.
NFPA 1710 covers career departments; NFPA 1720 covers volunteer departments.
Home fire inspections conflict with the Fourth Amendment and are too costly.
Risk = probability of an undesired event × severity of the consequence.
Watch most closely for risks that are high probability and high consequence.
All-hazard planning requires agreeing on lead agencies and communications interoperability before an incident.
remember: NFPA 1710 = career departments; NFPA 1720 = volunteer departments; NFPA 1500 = occupational safety and health program.
Three control measures: administrative, engineering, personnel protection.
Four steps of community risk reduction: preparation, mitigation, response, recovery.

sections.heading: The Future of Fire Protection
sections.simplified:
The term 'fire department' is becoming outdated. 'Emergency services agency' is more accurate, because apart from police work the fire department handles most public safety emergencies and many non-emergency functions too.

Worker safety is getting more attention, and OSHA regulations, found in the Code of Federal Regulations Title 29, Part 1910, will increasingly shape how much risk firefighters are allowed to take. Overall, the trend is toward fire prevention and away from manual suppression. Some expect future fire departments to act more like regulators of built-in protection systems, especially since modern building design makes fires harder to put out.
key_points: 'Emergency services agency' is a more accurate name than 'fire department.'
Except for police functions, the fire department handles most public safety emergencies.
OSHA rules (29 CFR Part 1910) will increasingly scrutinize firefighter risk-taking.
The trend is toward prevention and away from manual suppression.
remember: Future trend: toward prevention, away from manual suppression.
OSHA's rules are in 29 CFR Part 1910.

flashcards.front: What innovation gave birth to the interior attack?
flashcards.back: Extending a hose from the gooseneck so crews could apply water directly to the seat of the fire.

flashcards.front: What is a squirrel tail?
flashcards.back: A suction hose permanently attached to the pumper.

flashcards.front: Three advantages of the steamer?
flashcards.back: Only a three-person crew, could pump as long as there was coal, didn't need volunteers on the brakes.

flashcards.front: How did the chemical wagon create pressure?
flashcards.back: Mixing soda-water with acid produced carbon dioxide gas.

flashcards.front: Where does the name 'Maltese cross' come from?
flashcards.back: The Knights of St. John, headquartered on Malta, honored for bravery during the Crusades.

flashcards.front: Why were Dalmatians kept in firehouses?
flashcards.back: To guard horse-drawn vehicles and keep the horses calm.

flashcards.front: What did the 1904 Baltimore fire lead to?
flashcards.back: Standardized hose threads for firefighting equipment.

flashcards.front: When was the first National Fire Prevention Week, and who proclaimed it?
flashcards.back: October 4–10, 1925, by President Calvin Coolidge.

flashcards.front: Three common denominators of historic conflagrations?
flashcards.back: Combustible construction, narrow streets, ineffective building codes.

flashcards.front: What causes Santa Ana winds?
flashcards.back: High pressure over the Great Basin and low pressure off the Southern California coast.

flashcards.front: Leading cause of home fires and injuries?
flashcards.back: Cooking.

flashcards.front: Leading cause of fire deaths?
flashcards.back: Careless smoking.

flashcards.front: Leading cause of deaths, injuries, and dollar loss in commercial properties?
flashcards.back: Arson.

flashcards.front: What is the U.S. fire death rate?
flashcards.back: 13.1 per million population.

flashcards.front: By how much do residential sprinklers cut the home fire death rate?
flashcards.back: 74 percent.

flashcards.front: What is the main purpose of the fire service?
flashcards.back: To manage community risk.

flashcards.front: Define acceptable risk.
flashcards.back: Risk whose probability is so small, consequences so slight, or benefits so great that people are willing to accept it.

flashcards.front: What are the three categories of fire department risk?
flashcards.back: Community, organizational, and operational risk.

flashcards.front: What are the four goals of fire protection?
flashcards.back: Prevent fire from starting; prevent loss of life; confine fire to its origin; extinguish it.

flashcards.front: Policy vs. procedure?
flashcards.back: A policy is a general guideline; a procedure is a specific instruction for a recurring task.

flashcards.front: NFPA 1710 vs. NFPA 1720?
flashcards.back: 1710 covers career fire departments; 1720 covers volunteer departments.

flashcards.front: What are the three risk control measures?
flashcards.back: Administrative, engineering, and personnel protection.

flashcards.front: What are the four steps of community risk reduction?
flashcards.back: Preparation, mitigation, response, recovery.

flashcards.front: What name better describes the modern fire department?
flashcards.back: Emergency services agency.

quiz.question: Which city established the first publicly funded, paid fire department in America?
quiz.explanation: Boston did so in 1679. Cincinnati (1853) was the first fully paid department.

quiz.question: Who conceived the idea of the volunteer fire company in use today?
quiz.explanation: Franklin organized the Union Volunteer Fire Company in Philadelphia in 1736.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of the fire service according to the chapter?
quiz.explanation: The chapter states the main purpose is to manage community risk.

quiz.question: The 1904 Baltimore conflagration eventually led to:
quiz.explanation: Out-of-town crews' hoses didn't fit Baltimore's hydrants.

quiz.question: What is the leading cause of fire deaths in the United States?
quiz.explanation: Cooking leads home fires and injuries, but careless smoking leads fire deaths.

quiz.question: The greatest loss-of-life wildland fire in U.S. history occurred in:
quiz.explanation: The Peshtigo fire killed more than 1,500 people.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the four steps of community risk reduction?
quiz.explanation: The four steps are preparation, mitigation, response, and recovery.

quiz.question: Which NFPA standard addresses staffing and deployment for volunteer fire departments?
quiz.explanation: 1720 covers volunteer departments; 1710 covers career departments.

quiz.question: Standard operating procedures and training requirements are examples of which control measure?
quiz.explanation: Administrative controls are guidelines, policies, and procedures that limit losses.

quiz.question: Why did steamers contribute to the end of volunteer departments in large cities?
choices: They were too expensive to operate
They required only a small crew to run
They could not be pulled by horses
They needed a bucket brigade to fill
quiz.explanation: A three-person crew could run a steamer, so cities could afford small paid departments.

quiz.question: The Maltese cross originated with:
quiz.explanation: The Knights of St. John were headquartered on Malta.

quiz.question: After the Big Blowup of 1910, federal policy required wildland fires to be:
choices: Managed based on cost per acre
Put out by 10 a.m. the next day
quiz.explanation: The policy was to suppress all fires by 10 a.m. the following day.

quiz.question: Which of these is a common denominator of historic conflagrations?
quiz.explanation: The three are combustible construction, narrow streets, and ineffective building codes.

quiz.question: About what share of civilian fire deaths occur in the home?
quiz.explanation: 82% of civilian fire fatalities occur in the home.
